newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Audi seeks U.S. revival after sales plunge.
newsitem.headline: Audi seeks U.S. revival after sales plunge.

text.p: German car maker Audi AG is back on the road in the lucrative American market after recovering from a sharp slowdown in sales 10 years ago following allegations that its luxury sedan could have unintended acceleration problems.

U.S. officials cleared Audi of the allegations, made in a 1986 television programme, a few years later but the damage was done. Its U.S. sales skidded to 12,283 vehicles in 1991, when imported cars were also out of style, from a 1985 peak of more than 74,000.

But Audi's U.S. sales last year were the best in a decade, rising to 27,379 cars, which represented a doubling of sales in two years. The gains made Audi, part of the Volkswagen group, the fastest-growing luxury car maker in America.
Its current sales still lag those of the heady days of the 1980s but more good times appear to be ahead.
The company predicts another 20 percent growth in 1997 sales to slightly more than 30,000 vehicles.
"We still have a way to go and we will keep up the aggressive growth," Gerd Klauss, the architect of Audi's recovery in North America, said in a recent telephone interview from its Detroit office.

Renewed growth has come from strong consumer interest in Audi's A4 and A8 sedans. Audi officials hope to add fuel to the expansion with the new A6 sedan, which will be unveiled this week at the Geneva car show.

The A6 targets affluent buyers who are also considering such cars as the BMW 5-series and the Mercedes E-Class sedans. It will be available for German delivery in May and Audi will announce in Geneva when it will be sent to the U.S. market.

Audi has also spent tens of millions of dollars revamping its image, doubling its advertising budget in two years and expanding from traditional locations to mainstream publications such as Vanity Fair and Esquire in a broad-based campaign to reposition the Audi brand.

It has also side-stepped traditional advertising mediums and driven into prosperous areas such as Aspen, Colorado; Long Island, New York; Chicago and Miami with a plan to give top social leaders free use of an A8 for a month and then linked the vehicles to a major social event.
"We created a stir in the right circles with about 40 cars and created an immediate awareness for the vehicle," Klauss said. "It's been a success at getting high-profile customers."
Klauss, a former 18-year Mercedes-Benz executive, was named president of Audi's U.S. division in the early 1990s and given the task to revive it.
"It's now history but it was an undeserved hit below the belt," Klauss said about the dramatic drop in sales. "But we are moving forward."
Klauss moved quickly to put Audi's production in order, slashing a revamped model line in half.
"We wanted to take advantage of economies of scale and also provide a better value for consumers. We listened to them and could give them what they really wanted," Klauss said.

One step was to offer the Audi quattro all-wheel-drive system as an individual option instead of as a packaged group option to combat popular sport-utility vehicles. The result -- the quattro option is now sold on 70 percent of all vehicles.
"We finally gave the customers what they wanted," said Klauss with a sigh of relief. "Why be stuck with a truck when you can have the same security and safety in a passenger car?"
But Klauss knows the work is not finished, saying Audi must intensify efforts at rebuilding its dealer network to create more of a luxury-brand image and building sales volumes.

"We still have to be sensitive about building the brand image and brand awareness," Klauss said. "We have fantastic ownership loyalty but we have to tell the broader world what we stand for. We are gaining ground but it will take time."
